concepts: Non-trivial solution of a homogeneous system
General solution of tan θ = k
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all values of $\theta\in[-\pi,\pi]$ for which the system of linear equations $x+y+\sqrt3 z=0$, $-x+(\tan\theta)y+\sqrt7 z=0$, $x+y+(\tan\theta)z=0$ has a non-trivial solution. Then $\frac{120}{\pi}\sum_{\theta\in S}\theta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: A non-trivial solution needs $D=0$; subtracting $R_1$ from $R_3$ makes the determinant factorise as $(\tan\theta-\sqrt3)(\tan\theta+1)$.
solution: For a non-trivial solution of the homogeneous system, $D=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract equations 1 and 3 to get $(\tan\theta-\sqrt3)z=0$, then split into the cases $z\ne0$ and $z=0$.
solution: Case $z\ne0$: $\tan\theta=\sqrt3$. The system becomes $x+y+\sqrt3z=0$, $-x+\sqrt3y+\sqrt7z=0$ (equation 3 repeats equation 1): two equations in three unknowns, so a non-zero solution exists.
Case $z=0$: $x+y=0$ and $-x+(\tan\theta)y=0$ give $(\tan\theta+1)y=0$; a non-zero solution needs $y\ne0$, i.e. $\tan\theta=-1$.
So $\tan\theta\in\{\sqrt3,-1\}$ exactly, and the number $\sqrt7$ plays no role.
In $[-\pi,\pi]$: $\theta=\frac\pi3,-\frac{2\pi}3,-\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4$ with sum $\frac\pi6$, so the value is $\frac{120}\pi\cdot\frac\pi6=20$.

useful_results: A homogeneous system $AX=0$ has a non-trivial solution iff $|A|=0$. Subtracting rows that share most entries (here $R_3-R_1=(0,0,\tan\theta-\sqrt3)$) factorises the determinant at once: $|A|=(\tan\theta-\sqrt3)(\tan\theta+1)$.
Solutions of $\tan\theta=k$ in $[-\pi,\pi]$ are $\theta_0$ and $\theta_0-\pi$ (here $\frac\pi3,-\frac{2\pi}3$ and $\frac{3\pi}4,-\frac\pi4$): each tangent value gives two angles that differ by $\pi$.
Pairs $\theta_0,\theta_0-\pi$ sum to $2\theta_0-\pi$, so $\sum\theta=(2\cdot\frac\pi3-\pi)+(2\cdot\frac{3\pi}4-\pi)=-\frac\pi3+\frac\pi2=\frac\pi6$.

concepts: Matrix equation and unique solution of a linear system
questions.question: Let $A$ be a $3\times3$ real matrix such that $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $A\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}=4\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $A\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}=2\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$. Then the system $(A-3I)\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ has :
questions.key_idea: The three relations pin down every entry of $A$, and $A-3I$ comes out as an invertible anti-diagonal matrix.
solution: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}x_1&y_1&z_1\\x_2&y_2&z_2\\x_3&y_3&z_3\end{pmatrix}$ and use the three given relations.
$A(0,1,0)^T=(0,2,0)^T$ gives the middle column: $y_1=0,\ y_2=2,\ y_3=0$.
Row 1: adding the two equations gives $2z_1=-2$, so $z_1=-1$ and $x_1=3$.
Row 2: $x_2=z_2=0$. Row 3: adding gives $2z_3=6$, so $z_3=3$ and $x_3=-1$.
The system reads $-z=1,\ -y=2,\ -x=3$ (rows 1, 2, 3), so $z=-1,\ y=-2,\ x=-3$.
$|A-3I|=1\ne0$, so $A-3I$ is invertible and the solution $(-3,-2,-1)$ is unique.
questions.correction_note: PDF's last lines read $-z=3\Rightarrow z=-3$ and $-x=1\Rightarrow x=-1$, i.e. the right-hand sides of rows 1 and 3 were swapped. Correct: row 1 is $-z=1$ and row 3 is $-x=3$, so the solution is $(x,y,z)=(-3,-2,-1)$ (verified: $(A-3I)(-3,-2,-1)^T=(1,2,3)^T$). The conclusion (unique solution, option D) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The relations say $A$ has eigenvalues $2,4,2$ on a basis, so $A-3I$ has eigenvalues $-1,1,-1$: invertible, with no need to find $A$.
solution: The relations are $Av_i=\lambda_iv_i$ with $v_1=(1,0,1)^T,\ v_2=(-1,0,1)^T,\ v_3=(0,1,0)^T$ and $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3=2,4,2$.
The determinant of the matrix with columns $v_1,v_2,v_3$ is $-2\ne0$, so $v_1,v_2,v_3$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Then $(A-3I)v_i=(\lambda_i-3)v_i$: in this basis $A-3I$ is diagonal with entries $-1,\ 1,\ -1$.
An invertible coefficient matrix gives exactly one solution of $(A-3I)X=b$ for any $b$, so the system has a unique solution: (D).

useful_results: $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ means $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue; $A-cI$ has eigenvalues $\lambda-c$, so $A-cI$ is singular iff $c$ is an eigenvalue of $A$. Here $3\notin\{2,4\}$, so $A-3I$ is invertible.
A $3\times3$ matrix is fixed by its action on three independent vectors: $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $P=[v_1\,v_2\,v_3]$. (Here $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&-1\\0&2&0\\-1&0&3\end{pmatrix}$.)
$(A-cI)X=b$ has a unique solution for every $b$ iff $c$ is not an eigenvalue; if $c$ is an eigenvalue it has no solution or infinitely many, depending on $b$.

concepts: Adjoint and determinant of a matrix
questions.question: If $A$ is a square matrix of order $3$ such that $\det(A)=3$ and $\det\!\left(\operatorname{adj}\!\left(-4\operatorname{adj}\!\left(-3\operatorname{adj}\!\left(3\operatorname{adj}\!\left((2A)^{-1}\right)\right)\right)\right)\right)=2^m3^n$, then $m+2n$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: For order 3, $|\operatorname{adj}M|=|M|^2$ and $|kM|=k^3|M|$: each adjoint squares the determinant and each scalar cubes itself.
solution: For a $3\times3$ matrix, $|\operatorname{adj}M|=|M|^2$ and $|kM|=k^3|M|$. Let $P=3\operatorname{adj}((2A)^{-1})$ and $Q=-3\operatorname{adj}P$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\operatorname{adj}M=|M|M^{-1}$ and $\operatorname{adj}(kM)=k^2\operatorname{adj}M$ to turn every layer into a scalar multiple of $A$ or $A^{-1}$, then take one determinant.

useful_results: For an $n\times n$ matrix: $|\operatorname{adj}M|=|M|^{n-1}$, $|kM|=k^n|M|$, $\operatorname{adj}(kM)=k^{n-1}\operatorname{adj}M$, $\operatorname{adj}M=|M|M^{-1}$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=|M|^{n-2}M$.

Repeating adj $j$ times multiplies the exponent: $|\operatorname{adj}^{(j)}M|=|M|^{(n-1)^j}$; for $n=3$ the exponent doubles each time ($|\operatorname{adj}\operatorname{adj}\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^8$).
Strategy: track the determinant layer by layer from the inside, or rewrite each layer as (scalar)$\cdot A^{\pm1}$ and take a single determinant at the end.

concepts: Determinant condition and powers of an idempotent matrix
Binomial expansion
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&-1\\6&\beta\end{pmatrix}$, $\alpha>0$, such that $\det(A)=0$ and $\alpha+\beta=1$. If $I$ denotes the $2\times2$ identity matrix, then the matrix $(I+A)^8$ is :
questions.key_idea: $\alpha\beta=-6$ and $\alpha+\beta=1$ give $A^2=A$, so $(I+A)^8=I+(2^8-1)A$.
solution: With $\alpha+\beta=1$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $t^2-t-6=0$, i.e. $3$ and $-2$; since $\alpha>0$, $\alpha=3,\ \beta=-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cayley-Hamilton gives $A^2=A$ straight from $\operatorname{tr}A=1$, $|A|=0$; then $(I+A)^k=I+(2^k-1)A$ by induction.
solution: Cayley-Hamilton: $A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+|A|I=0$. Here $\operatorname{tr}A=\alpha+\beta=1$ and $|A|=0$, so $A^2=A$ (before even finding $\alpha,\beta$).
If $(I+A)^k=I+(2^k-1)A$, then $(I+A)^{k+1}=\left(I+(2^k-1)A\right)(I+A)=I+A+(2^k-1)A+(2^k-1)A^2=I+(2^{k+1}-1)A$. So the formula holds for all $k$.

useful_results: Idempotent matrix ($A^2=A$): $(I+A)^n=I+(2^n-1)A$ and more generally $(xI+yA)^n=x^nI+\left((x+y)^n-x^n\right)A$. Eigenvalues of $A$ are $0,1$.
For any $2\times2$ matrix, $A^2=(\operatorname{tr}A)A-|A|I$. If $\operatorname{tr}A=1$ and $|A|=0$ then $A$ is idempotent.
Always test $A^2$ early: if it equals $A$ (or $0$, or $I$) all higher powers collapse and the binomial expansion becomes a single sum such as $\sum_{r\ge1}{}^nC_r=2^n-1$.

concepts: Exponential equation reducible to a quadratic
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}:(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^x+(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)^x=10\right\}$. Then the number of elements in $S$ is :
questions.key_idea: $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)=1$, so with $t=(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^x$ the equation is $t+\frac1t=10$.
solution: Taking the $+$ sign gives $x=2$; the $-$ sign gives $(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)^2=(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^{-2}$, so $x=-2$.
Hence $x=2$ or $x=-2$: the number of solutions is $2$. Option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: $f(x)=u^x+u^{-x}$ is even and strictly increasing for $x>0$, so $f(x)=10$ has exactly one positive and one negative root.
solution: Put $u=\sqrt3+\sqrt2>1$; then $\sqrt3-\sqrt2=u^{-1}$ and the equation is $f(x)=u^x+u^{-x}=10$.
$f(-x)=f(x)$: the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, and $f(0)=2<10$, so $0\notin S$.
For $x>0$: $f'(x)=\ln u\,(u^x-u^{-x})>0$, so $f$ increases from $2$ to $\infty$ and takes the value $10$ exactly once.
By symmetry there is exactly one negative root as well, so $|S|=2$.

useful_results: If $ab=1$ then $a^x+b^x=t+\frac1t$ with $t=a^x$: such equations reduce to $t^2-ct+1=0$ and have the two roots $t,\frac1t$, giving solutions $\pm x_0$ (for $c>2$).
$t+\frac1t\ge2$ for $t>0$ with equality only at $t=1$; so $a^x+a^{-x}=c$ has two real solutions iff $c>2$, one ($x=0$) iff $c=2$, none iff $c<2$.
Recognise the conjugate pair: $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^2=5+2\sqrt6$ and $(5+2\sqrt6)(5-2\sqrt6)=1$; also $(a+\sqrt{b})^n+(a-\sqrt b)^n$ is always an integer.

concepts: Infinite series of reciprocal fourth powers (odd and even terms)
questions.question: If $\frac1{1^4}+\frac1{2^4}+\frac1{3^4}+\dots\infty=\frac{\pi^4}{90}$, $\ \frac1{1^4}+\frac1{3^4}+\frac1{5^4}+\dots\infty=\alpha$, $\ \frac1{2^4}+\frac1{4^4}+\frac1{6^4}+\dots\infty=\beta$, then $\frac\alpha\beta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The even-index terms are $\frac1{2^4}$ times the whole series, so $\beta=\frac S{16}$ and $\alpha=S-\beta$.
solution: Odd terms plus even terms make the whole series: $\alpha+\frac1{2^4}\left(\frac{\pi^4}{90}\right)=\frac{\pi^4}{90}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the total as $\frac{\pi^2}{90}$ (and $\alpha=\frac{\pi^2}{90}\cdot\frac{15}{16}$) although the series sum is $\frac{\pi^4}{90}$; the exponent is a typo. It cancels in $\frac\alpha\beta$, so the answer 15 (C) is unchanged.
useful_results: For $\sum\frac1{n^p}=S$: the even-index part is $\frac S{2^p}$ and the odd-index part is $S\left(1-\frac1{2^p}\right)$, so $\frac{\text{odd}}{\text{even}}=2^p-1$ ($p=4$: $15$; $p=2$: $3$).

Known values: $\sum\frac1{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}6$, $\sum\frac1{n^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90}$. Odd-only: $\sum\frac1{(2k-1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8$, $\sum\frac1{(2k-1)^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{96}$ (indeed $\frac{\pi^4}{90}\cdot\frac{15}{16}=\frac{\pi^4}{96}$).
Alternating version: $\sum\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^4}=S-2\beta=S\left(1-\frac18\right)=\frac{7\pi^4}{720}$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression
Geometric progression
questions.question: Let $2^{nd}$, $8^{th}$ and $44^{th}$ terms of a non-constant A.P. be respectively the $1^{st}$, $2^{nd}$ and $3^{rd}$ terms of a G.P. If the first term of the A.P. is $1$, then the sum of its first $20$ terms is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Three terms in G.P. means (middle)$^2$ = (product of the outer two), which gives $d=5a$.
solution: Let the A.P. have first term $a$ and common difference $d$. Its $2^{nd},8^{th},44^{th}$ terms $a+d,\ a+7d,\ a+43d$ are the $1^{st},2^{nd},3^{rd}$ terms of a G.P.
The A.P. is non-constant, so $d\ne0$; with $a=1$ we get $d=5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In a G.P. the ratio of consecutive differences equals the common ratio, and here those differences are $6d$ and $36d$.

useful_results: If AP terms $t_p,t_q,t_r$ are in G.P. (non-constant AP), the G.P. ratio is $\frac{r-q}{q-p}$; here $\frac{44-8}{8-2}=6$.
Then $\frac{a+(q-1)d}{a+(p-1)d}=\frac{r-q}{q-p}$ links $a$ and $d$ linearly; here $a+7d=6(a+d)\Rightarrow d=5a$.
Quick check of the answer: terms $6,36,216$ are in G.P. with ratio $6$; $S_n=\frac n2[2a+(n-1)d]=\frac{n(5n-3)}2$ gives $S_{20}=\frac{20\cdot97}2=970$.

concepts: Consistency of a 3×3 system with infinitely many solutions
questions.question: If the system of equations $(\lambda-1)x+(\lambda-4)y+\lambda z=5$, $\ \lambda x+(\lambda-1)y+(\lambda-4)z=7$, $\ (\lambda+1)x+(\lambda+2)y-(\lambda+2)z=9$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\lambda^2+\lambda$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $D=0$ is only necessary: both roots of $D=0$ must be tested for consistency, and only $\lambda=3$ survives.
solution: Expanding along $R_2$: $(2\lambda-6)(-\lambda-2+3\lambda+3)=0$, i.e. $(\lambda-3)(2\lambda+1)=0$ up to sign.
Consistency check: at $\lambda=3$, row 3 $=-$row 1 $+\,2\,$row 2 on the left and $-5+14=9$ on the right, so the system is consistent with rank 2: infinitely many solutions.
At $\lambda=-\frac12$ the coefficient matrix has rank 2 but the augmented matrix has rank 3: no solution. So only $\lambda=3$ is admissible.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops at $D=0$ and says $\lambda=3$ or $-\frac12$, then evaluates only $\lambda=3$ without rejecting $-\frac12$. $D=0$ is necessary, not sufficient: at $\lambda=-\frac12$ the system is inconsistent (no solution), so only $\lambda=3$ gives infinitely many solutions. This consistency check was added; the answer 12 (B) is unchanged. (Also the PDF's expansion drops a cofactor sign, which does not affect $=0$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Add (E1$-$E2) and (E3$-$E2): the unknowns $x,y$ cancel and leave $(6-2\lambda)z=0$, which separates the cases and shows consistency directly.
solution:
If $\lambda
e3$: $z=0$, so $x+3y=2$; E2 becomes $\lambda x+(\lambda-1)y=7$. Two equations in $x,y$ are either independent (one solution) or, if proportional, need $\lambda:(\lambda-1)=1:3$, i.e. $\lambda=- rac12$, but then the right side would have to be $2\lambda=-1
e7$: no solution. So no $\lambda
e3$ gives infinitely many solutions.
If $\lambda=3$: the sum is $0=0$, so E3$-$E2 $=-($E1$-$E2$)$ and the three equations reduce to two independent consistent ones in three unknowns: infinitely many solutions.

useful_results: For a square system, $D=0$ only means 'no unique solution': you must still check consistency (compare ranks of coefficient and augmented matrices, or show a combination of equations gives $0=0$ rather than $0=c\ne0$).
When $D=0$ has several roots in a parameter, typically exactly one gives infinitely many solutions and the others give none; here $\lambda=3$ versus $\lambda=-\frac12$.
Adding/subtracting equations to cancel unknowns (here E1$-$E2 and E3$-$E2) is faster than a $3\times3$ determinant with parameters.

concepts: Common terms of two arithmetic progressions
Cardinality of a union of sets
questions.question: Let $A=\{1,6,11,16,\dots\}$ and $B=\{9,16,23,30,\dots\}$ be the sets consisting of the first $2025$ terms of two arithmetic progressions. Then $n(A\cup B)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Common terms of two APs form an AP with difference $\operatorname{lcm}(d_1,d_2)$, and are limited by the shorter range; then use $n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)$.
solution: $A$ has first term $1$ and $d_1=5$; $B$ has first term $9$ and $d_2=7$; each has $2025$ terms.
$\operatorname{lcm}(d_1,d_2)=35$, so the common terms form the sequence $16,51,86,\dots$ (difference $35$).
The last term of $A$ is $1+(2025-1)\cdot5=10121$; the last term of $B$ is $9+2024\cdot7=14177>10121$, so $A$ limits the common terms.
questions.correction_note: The PDF ends at '$n=289$' (the number of common terms) and never computes $n(A\cup B)$; it also does not check that the common terms lie within $B$'s range. The last two steps (B's last term $14177>10121$ and $2025+2025-289=3761$) were added. Answer (A) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count common elements by congruence: every term of $B$ is $\equiv2\pmod7$, so count the terms $1+5k$ of $A$ that are $\equiv2\pmod 7$.
solution: $A=\{1+5k:0\le k\le2024\}$ and every element of $B=\{9+7j\}$ is $\equiv2\pmod7$.
So $k=3+7m$ with $3+7m\le2024$, i.e. $m=0,1,\dots,288$: that is $289$ values.
For these terms $16\le x\le10121$, and $9\le x\le14177$, so each lies in the range of $B$ too: $n(A\cap B)=289$.

useful_results: Two APs $a_1+(m-1)d_1$ and $a_2+(n-1)d_2$ share terms iff $a_1\equiv a_2\pmod{\gcd(d_1,d_2)}$; the common terms then form an AP with difference $\operatorname{lcm}(d_1,d_2)$ (here $35$).

For finite APs the common terms must lie between $\max$(first terms) and $\min$(last terms); count them by $\left\lfloor\frac{\text{last bound}-\text{first common}}{\operatorname{lcm}}\right\rfloor+1$.
Then $n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)$. Small check: $A=\{1,6,11,16\}$, $B=\{9,16\}$ share only $16$, so $n(A\cup B)=4+2-1=5$.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a 3×3 linear system
questions.question: If the system of equations $x+2y-3z=2$, $\ 2x+\lambda y+5z=5$, $\ 14x+3y+\mu z=33$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\lambda+\mu$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions force $D_y=D_z=0$, and these two minors give $\mu$ and $\lambda$ directly.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $x$ by row operations; infinitely many solutions need the two remaining equations in $y,z$ to be proportional (right side included).
solution: The system has infinitely many solutions iff these two equations are proportional, constants included: $\frac{\lambda-4}{-25}=\frac{11}{\mu+42}=\frac15$.

useful_results: For a $3\times3$ system, infinitely many solutions $\iff$ rank of coefficient matrix = rank of augmented matrix $=2$ (or $1$). After eliminating one variable, the two leftover equations must be proportional including the right-hand sides.
With Cramer's rule, $D=0$ and any one $D_i\ne0$ means no solution; all four zero is necessary but one should still confirm rank 2 (here the rows are not proportional, so rank is $2$).
Pick the cheapest determinants first: $D_y=\mu-13$ and $D_z=5\lambda+5$ are linear and give the parameters at once, so $D$ itself need not be expanded.

concepts: Sum of a series using Σr and Σr²
questions.question: $1^2+3+5^2+7+9^2+\dots$ up to $40$ terms is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Split into squares of $4r-3$ and plain terms $4r-1$ for $r=1,\dots,20$, then use $\sum r$ and $\sum r^2$.
useful_results: A series that alternates between two patterns (square, plain, square, plain, ...) is split by position parity into two simple series, each of half the length.
Standard sums: $\sum_{r=1}^nr=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, $\sum_{r=1}^nr^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$; for $n=20$: $210$ and $2870$.

concepts: Logarithms in A.P. and G.P. relations
questions.question: If $\log_ea,\ \log_eb,\ \log_ec$ are in A.P. and $\log_ea-\log_e2b,\ \log_e2b-\log_e3c,\ \log_e3c-\log_ea$ are also in an A.P., then $a:b:c$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Logs in A.P. means the numbers are in G.P.; apply it to $\frac a{2b},\frac{2b}{3c},\frac{3c}a$.
solution: Also $\log_e\frac a{2b},\ \log_e\frac{2b}{3c},\ \log_e\frac{3c}a$ are in A.P., so $\left(\frac{2b}{3c}\right)^2=\frac a{2b}\cdot\frac{3c}a$.
The right side is $\frac{3c}{2b}$, so $(2b)^3=(3c)^3$ and $\frac bc=\frac32$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $a,b,c$ as a G.P. $p,pr,pr^2$, so every ratio is a power of $r$ and one cubic in $r$ remains.
solution: From the first A.P., $a,b,c$ are in G.P.: $a=p,\ b=pr,\ c=pr^2$.
A.P. of logs means (middle)$^2$ = (product of outer two): $\frac4{9r^2}=\frac1{2r}\cdot3r^2=\frac{3r}2$.

useful_results: $\log x,\log y,\log z$ are in A.P. $\iff x,y,z$ are in G.P. (for positive $x,y,z$): $y^2=xz$.
A list of three positive numbers in G.P. can always be written $p,pr,pr^2$; ratios of such terms depend only on $r$, which reduces many 'ratio of three numbers' questions to one equation.
Check: $(a,b,c)=(9,6,4)$ gives $b^2=36=ac$ and the ratios $\frac a{2b}=\frac34,\ \frac{2b}{3c}=1,\ \frac{3c}a=\frac43$ in G.P. (middle$^2=1=\frac34\cdot\frac43$).

concepts: Roots of a quadratic with coefficient sum zero
AM–GM inequality
questions.question: For $0<c<b<a$, let $(a+b-2c)x^2+(b+c-2a)x+(c+a-2b)=0$ and $\alpha\ne1$ be one of its roots. Then, among the two statements: (I) If $\alpha\in(-1,0)$, then $b$ cannot be the geometric mean of $a$ and $c$. (II) If $\alpha\in(0,1)$, then $b$ may be the geometric mean of $a$ and $c$.
questions.key_idea: The coefficients sum to $0$, so $1$ is a root and $\alpha$ is the product of roots; the sign of $\alpha$ compares $b$ with $\frac{a+c}2$.
solution: The coefficients add up to $(a+b-2c)+(b+c-2a)+(c+a-2b)=0$, so $x=1$ is a root, and the other root is $\alpha\ne1$.
Since $c<a$ and $c<b$, $2c<a+b$, so the denominator $a+b-2c$ is positive.
The right inequality gives $2b>a+c$, i.e. $b>\frac{a+c}2$ (the left one reduces to $b+c<2a$, always true as $b<a,\ c<a$).
Since $\sqrt{ac}<\frac{a+c}2$ (G.M. < A.M. for $a\ne c$), we get $b>\frac{a+c}2>\sqrt{ac}$, so $b$ cannot be the G.M. of $a,c$: (I) is true.
So $b<\frac{a+c}2$, which leaves room for $b=\sqrt{ac}$; for instance $a=4,\ b=2,\ c=1$ has $0<c<b<a$, $b=\sqrt{ac}$ and $\alpha=\frac{1+4-4}{4+2-2}=\frac14\in(0,1)$. So (II) is true.
questions.correction_note: The PDF shows $b<\frac{a+c}2$ and writes 'G.M. < A.M., so $b$ may be the G.M.' but never shows that $b=\sqrt{ac}$ is actually attainable with $0<c<b<a$; the example $a=4,b=2,c=1$ ($\alpha=\frac14$) was added. Also note: the Hindi version of the options in the PDF is in a different order (A) both, (B) only I, (C) only II, (D) neither, while the English order (D = both) matches the printed key D; the English order is followed here.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $x=a-b>0$ and $y=b-c>0$: then $\alpha=\frac{x-y}{x+2y}$, so the sign of $\alpha$ is the sign of $x-y$.
solution: $1$ is a root (coefficients sum to $0$) and $\alpha=\frac{c+a-2b}{a+b-2c}$.
$-1<\alpha<0\iff x<y$ (the bound $\alpha>-1$ holds automatically as $2x+y>0$). And $x<y\iff a-b<b-c\iff2b>a+c$, so $b>\frac{a+c}2\ge\sqrt{ac}$: $b\ne\sqrt{ac}$, (I) true.

$0<\alpha<1\iff x>y$ (the bound $\alpha<1$ holds as $y>0$) $\iff2b<a+c$: $b$ lies below the A.M., and the G.M. does too, so $b=\sqrt{ac}$ is possible: $a=4,b=2,c=1$ gives $x=2,y=1,\alpha=\frac14$. (II) true.

useful_results: If the coefficients of $px^2+qx+r$ add to $0$, then $1$ is a root and the other root is $\frac rp$; if $p-q+r=0$ then $-1$ is a root.
For $a>b>c>0$, put $x=a-b,\ y=b-c$: then $2b\gtrless a+c\iff y\gtrless x$, so questions about $b$ versus the A.M. become a comparison of two positive gaps.

For positive $a\ne c$: $\sqrt{ac}<\frac{a+c}2$ (G.M. < A.M.). So $b\ge\frac{a+c}2$ always excludes $b=\sqrt{ac}$, while $b<\frac{a+c}2$ merely allows it (verified: $(10,9,1)$ has $\alpha=-\frac7{17}\in(-1,0)$ and $b=9>5.5$).

concepts: Power sums of roots and quadratic with reciprocal roots
questions.question: Let $P_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n,\ n\in\mathbb{N}$. If $P_{10}=123,\ P_9=76,\ P_8=47$ and $P_1=1$, then the quadratic equation having roots $\frac1\alpha$ and $\frac1\beta$ is :
questions.key_idea: $P_{10}=P_9+P_8$ with $P_1=\alpha+\beta=1$ forces $\alpha\beta=-1$; reciprocal roots then have sum $-1$ and product $-1$.
solution: The recurrence $P_{n+2}=(\alpha+\beta)P_{n+1}-\alpha\beta P_n$ with $\alpha+\beta=1$ gives $123=76-47\,\alpha\beta$, so $\alpha\beta=-1$; i.e. $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy $x^2=x+1$, $x^2-x-1=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF jumps from '$P_{10}=P_9+P_8$' to '$x^2=x+1$' without justification (the equality of three numbers alone does not show that $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy $x^2=x+1$). The justification via $P_{n+2}=(\alpha+\beta)P_{n+1}-\alpha\beta P_n$ with $\alpha+\beta=1$ was added; result and answer (D) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reversing the coefficients of a polynomial gives the polynomial whose roots are the reciprocals.
solution: If $f$ has roots $\alpha,\beta\ne0$ then $x^2f\!\left(\frac1x\right)=1-x-x^2$ has roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta$ (reverse the coefficient list).

useful_results: Power sums satisfy $P_{n+2}=sP_{n+1}-pP_n$ with $s=\alpha+\beta,\ p=\alpha\beta$; any three consecutive values plus $s$ determine $p$.
To get the equation with roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta$: reverse the coefficients, $ax^2+bx+c\to cx^2+bx+a$ (here $x^2-x-1\to-x^2-x+1$). Roots $k\alpha,k\beta$: replace $x$ by $\frac xk$.
Here $\alpha,\beta=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}2$ (golden ratio), $P_n$ are Lucas numbers $1,3,4,7,11,\dots$: $P_8=47,\ P_9=76,\ P_{10}=123$ ✓.

concepts: Linear recurrence relation and sum of a sequence
questions.question: Let $\langle a_n\rangle$ be a sequence such that $a_0=0,\ a_1=\frac12$ and $2a_{n+2}=5a_{n+1}-3a_n,\ n=0,1,2,3,\dots$. Then $\sum_{k=1}^{100}a_k$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The characteristic roots are $1$ and $\frac32$, so $a_n=\left(\frac32\right)^n-1$ and the sum is a G.P. sum minus $100$.
solution: $a_0=0,\ a_1=\frac12,\ 2a_{n+2}=5a_{n+1}-3a_n$; the characteristic equation is $2x^2-5x+3=0$, so $x=1,\frac32$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The quantity $2a_{n+1}-3a_n$ is invariant, so $b_n=a_n+1$ is a G.P. and the sum telescopes against itself.
solution: Hence $a_{n+1}+1=\frac{3a_n+1}2+1=\frac32(a_n+1)$: $b_n=a_n+1$ is a G.P. with ratio $\frac32$ and $b_0=1$.

useful_results: For $pa_{n+2}=qa_{n+1}-ra_n$ with $p-q+r=0$ ($x=1$ is a characteristic root), the recurrence reduces to first order: $d_n=a_{n+1}-a_n$ satisfies $2d_{n+1}=3d_n$ here, a G.P. of differences.

If the roots are $1$ and $\rho$, then $a_n=A+B\rho^n$ and $\sum_{k=1}^N\rho^k=\frac{\rho(\rho^N-1)}{\rho-1}$; for $\rho=\frac32$ this is $3\left(\left(\frac32\right)^N-1\right)=3a_N$ when $a_N=\left(\frac32\right)^N-1$, which is why the answer is written through $a_{100}$.
Check: $a_2=\frac54,\ a_3=\frac{19}8$: $a_1+a_2+a_3=\frac12+\frac54+\frac{19}8=\frac{33}8$ and $3a_3-3=\frac{57}8-\frac{24}8=\frac{33}8$ ✓ (the same identity $\sum_{k\le N}a_k=3a_N-N$).

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a 3×3 system and solving a 2×2 system
questions.question: Let the system of linear equations $x+y+kz=2$, $\ 2x+3y-z=1$, $\ 3x+4y+2z=k$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the system $(k+1)x+(2k-1)y=7$, $\ (2k+1)x+(k+5)y=10$ has :
questions.key_idea: $D=0$ gives $k=3$; at $k=3$ subtracting the two equations of the second system gives $x+y=1$ immediately.
solution: Consistency: at $k=3$, row 3 $=$ row 1 + row 2 on the left $(3,4,2)$ and on the right $2+1=3=k$, so the system is consistent: infinitely many solutions indeed.
For $k=3$ the second system is $4x+5y=7$ ...(1) and $7x+8y=10$ ...(2).
Its determinant is $4\cdot8-5\cdot7=-3\ne0$, so it has a unique solution.
questions.correction_note: The PDF finds $k=3$ from $D=0$ but does not check consistency of the first system (needed because $D=0$ alone does not guarantee infinitely many solutions); the check (row 3 = row 1 + row 2 with $2+1=3=k$) was added. Also the PDF expansion line '$1(10)-1(7)+k(-1)-0$' has a stray '$-0$'. Answer (D) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Combine E1 + E2 $-$ E3 to get $(k-3)(z+1)=0$: it shows at once that only $k=3$ gives a dependent system.
solution: If $k\ne3$: $z=-1$, and E1, E2 become $x+y=2+k,\ 2x+3y=0$, which have a unique $(x,y)$: exactly one solution, not infinitely many.
If $k=3$: the combination is $0=0$, so E3 is the sum of E1 and E2 (right sides $2+1=3=k$): two independent equations in three unknowns, infinitely many solutions. Hence $k=3$.
Second system at $k=3$: $4x+5y=7,\ 7x+8y=10$. Subtracting: $3x+3y=3\Rightarrow x+y=1$; determinant $-3\ne0$, so the solution is unique. Option (D).

useful_results: A system is dependent when a combination of equations (on both sides) is $0=0$; finding it (here E3 = E1 + E2) is faster than a determinant and checks consistency at the same time.
Since the options mention $x-y$ or $x+y$, subtract or add the two equations first: $(7x+8y)-(4x+5y)=3x+3y$.
For $2\times2$ systems $a_1x+b_1y=c_1,\ a_2x+b_2y=c_2$: unique iff $a_1b_2\ne a_2b_1$; here $4\cdot8-5\cdot7=-3$.

concepts: Determinant of repeated adjoint
Sum over a solution set of a quadratic equation
questions.question: Let $A$ be a $3\times3$ matrix such that $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A))|=81$. If $S=\left\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:\left(|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|\right)^{\frac{(n-1)^2}2}=|A|^{3n^2-5n-4}\right\}$, then $\sum_{n\in S}\left|A^{(n^2+n)}\right|$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $|\operatorname{adj}\operatorname{adj}\operatorname{adj}A|=|\operatorname{adj}A|^4$ gives $|A|^2=3$; equating exponents then reduces $S$ to the quadratic $n^2-n-6=0$.
solution: Since $|A|=\pm\sqrt3$ has modulus $\ne1$, the exponents must be equal: $2(n-1)^2=3n^2-5n-4$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $|A|^2=3\Rightarrow|A|=\sqrt3$, dropping $|A|=-\sqrt3$. This is harmless: both exponents $12$ and $2$ are even, so the sum is $3^6+3=732$ for either sign. The PDF's first line also has a typographical slip '$|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj})(\operatorname{adj}A)|$'. Answer (D) unchanged.
useful_results: For order $n$: $|\operatorname{adj}M|=|M|^{n-1}$, and repeating $j$ times gives $|M|^{(n-1)^j}$. For $n=3$: $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^2$, $|\operatorname{adj}\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^4$, $|\operatorname{adj}^{(3)}A|=|A|^8$.
$a^x=a^y$ with $a>0,\ a\ne1$ (or $|a|\ne1$ in absolute-value form) forces $x=y$: take equal exponents to reduce such sets to an integer quadratic.
$|A^k|=|A|^k$ for every integer $k$ (including negative); even powers of $|A|=\pm\sqrt3$ do not depend on the sign.

concepts: Geometric progression: terms and sum
questions.question: If the sum of the second, fourth and sixth terms of a G.P. of positive terms is $21$ and the sum of its eighth, tenth and twelfth terms is $15309$, then the sum of its first nine terms is :
questions.key_idea: Dividing the two given sums cancels the common factor $1+r^2+r^4$, leaving $r^6=729$.
solution: Let the G.P. have first term $a$ and ratio $r>0$: $ar+ar^3+ar^5=21$ ...(1).
Sum of the first nine terms $=a(1+r+r^2+\dots+r^8)=\frac1{13}\cdot\frac{3^9-1}2$.
$r^6=729$ gives $r=3$ (as in the main solution). From (1), $a(1+r^2+r^4)=\frac{21}r=7$.

useful_results: In a G.P., $t_{k+6}=r^6t_k$ for every $k$: the sum of the 8th, 10th, 12th terms is $r^6$ times the sum of the 2nd, 4th, 6th, so $r^6=\frac{15309}{21}=729$.
$S_n=a\frac{r^n-1}{r-1}$; here $\frac1{13}\cdot\frac{19682}{2}=757$ (check: terms $\frac1{13},\frac3{13},\dots$ with $S_9=\frac{19682}{26}$).

concepts: Classification of solutions of a 3×3 linear system
questions.question: For the system of linear equations $x+y+z=6$, $\ \alpha x+\beta y+7z=3$, $\ x+2y+3z=14$, which of the following is NOT true?
options: If $\alpha=\beta=7$, then the system has no solution.
If $\alpha=\beta$ and $\alpha\ne7$, then the system has a unique solution.
There is a unique point $(\alpha,\beta)$ on the line $x+2y+18=0$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions.
For every point $(\alpha,\beta)\ne(7,7)$ on the line $x-2y+7=0$, the system has infinitely many solutions.
questions.key_idea: Reduce to one equation $(\alpha-2\beta+7)z=2\alpha-8\beta+3$ and test each option against the three cases it gives.
solution: (C) Infinite solutions need $\alpha=2\beta-7$ and $2\alpha-8\beta+3=0$, i.e. $-4\beta-11=0$: $\beta=-\frac{11}4,\ \alpha=-\frac{25}2$, and this point satisfies $\alpha+2\beta+18=-12.5-5.5+18=0$. So exactly one such point lies on $x+2y+18=0$: true.

(D) On $x-2y+7=0$ we have $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$; infinitely many solutions occur only at the single point $\left(-\frac{25}2,-\frac{11}4\right)$. At $(7,7)$ and at all other points of the line there is no solution, so (D) is NOT true.
questions.correction_note: The PDF derives the three cases ($\alpha-2\beta+7\ne0$ unique, etc.) but stops there and never tests options (A)-(D), so it does not show why (D) is the 'NOT true' statement. Steps 7-10 (checking every option) were added. Answer (D) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Look for multipliers $p,q$ with $p\cdot$E1$+q\cdot$E3 $=$ E2 (left side): E2 depends on the others iff $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$, and the right side then fixes the second condition.
solution: Seek $p,q$ with $p(1,1,1)+q(1,2,3)=(\alpha,\beta,7)$: $p+q=\alpha,\ p+2q=\beta,\ p+3q=7$. The first two give $q=\beta-\alpha,\ p=2\alpha-\beta$.
The third equation then needs $p+3q=-\alpha+2\beta=7$, i.e. $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$. Otherwise the three rows are independent (the determinant is $2\beta-\alpha-7\ne0$): a unique solution.

If $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$, E2's left side is $p$E1$+q$E3, so E2 is consistent iff $6p+14q=3$. Here $6p+14q=12\alpha-6\beta+14\beta-14\alpha=-2\alpha+8\beta$, so the condition is $2\alpha-8\beta+3=0$ (infinite solutions); otherwise none.

Options: (A) $(7,7)$: first condition holds, $-2\cdot7+8\cdot7=42
e3$: none, true. (B) $\alpha= eta
e7$: $7-\alpha
e0$: unique, true. (C) Both conditions give the single point $\left(- rac{25}2,- rac{11}4ight)$ and it lies on $x+2y+18=0$: true.
(D) On the line $x-2y+7=0$ only the one point $\left(-\frac{25}2,-\frac{11}4\right)$ gives infinitely many solutions; the others, including $(7,7)$, give none. So (D) is NOT true.

useful_results: For $3\times3$ systems with parameters, express one equation as a combination of the other two (multipliers $p,q$): the coefficient condition gives the 'singular' line/curve, and the right-side condition picks the infinite-solution points on it.

Classification pattern: $\text{(coefficient condition)}\ne0\Rightarrow$ unique; $=0$ and $\text{(constant condition)}\ne0\Rightarrow$ none; both $=0\Rightarrow$ infinitely many. Here the conditions are $\alpha-2\beta+7$ and $2\alpha-8\beta+3$.

'NOT true' questions: test every option separately; a statement of the form 'for every point on a line the system has infinitely many solutions' fails because infinitely many solutions need two independent conditions (a single point).

concepts: Classification of solutions of a 3×3 linear system
questions.question: For the system of linear equations $2x+4y+2az=b$, $\ x+2y+3z=4$, $\ 2x-5y+2z=8$, which of the following is NOT correct?
options: It has infinitely many solutions if $a=3,\ b=8$
It has infinitely many solutions if $a=3,\ b=6$
questions.key_idea: $D=18(3-a)$: $a\ne3$ gives a unique solution, and $a=3$ gives infinitely many only if $b=8$.
solution: If $a=3,\ b\ne8$: $D=0$ but $D_2\ne0$, so no solution.
If $a=3,\ b=8$: $D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0$ (e.g. $D_1=152-216+64=0$) and the equations are consistent, so infinitely many solutions.
(C) $a=3,\ b=6$: $b\ne8$, so there is no solution; 'infinitely many' is NOT correct.
(D) $a=b=6$: $a\ne3$, unique: correct. The incorrect statement is (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF computes $D,D_1,D_2,D_3$ and states the three cases but never tests the four options (A)-(D), so it does not identify which statement is NOT correct. The option-by-option check (last three bullets) was added. Answer (C) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: E1 $-\,2\,$E2 cancels $x$ and $y$ together and leaves $(2a-6)z=b-8$, which classifies the whole system in one line.
solution: The first two coefficients of E1 are twice those of E2, so E1$-2\cdot$E2 gives $(2a-6)z=b-8$.

If $a\ne3$: $z=\frac{b-8}{2a-6}$ is determined; E2 and E3 then give $x,y$ uniquely since $\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\2&-5\end{vmatrix}=-9\ne0$. Unique solution for every $b$: options (A) $a=b=8$ and (D) $a=b=6$ are correct.
If $a=3,\ b=8$: E1 is $2\cdot$E2, so only E2 and E3 remain (two equations, three unknowns): infinitely many solutions, (B) correct.
If $a=3,\ b=6$: E1$-2$E2 reads $0=-2$, inconsistent: no solution. So 'infinitely many solutions' in (C) is NOT correct.

useful_results: When two equations have proportional left sides (here E1 and $2\cdot$E2 in $x,y$), subtract to isolate the remaining variable: $(2a-6)z=b-8$ immediately gives all three cases.

For a square system with parameters: $D\ne0\Rightarrow$ unique; $D=0$ and a consistent system $\Rightarrow$ infinitely many; $D=0$ and an inconsistent one $\Rightarrow$ none. Always test consistency separately when $D=0$.
Check for $a=3,\ b=8$: $(4,0,0)$ and $\left(\frac{17}9,-\frac49,1\right)$ both satisfy all three equations, so there is more than one solution (infinitely many).
